stories.headline: Trump Threatens 100 Percent Tariff on Countries That Tax U.S. Tech Firms
stories.summary:
President Trump on Friday threatened to impose a 100 percent tariff on imports from any country that levies a digital services tax on American technology companies, escalating trade tensions with Europe in particular. In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote: "Any Country that imposes such a Tax will immediately be met with a 100% TARIFF on any and all Goods sent to the United States of America," and stated the new tariff would supersede existing trade agreements.

The warning comes as several European nations have been discussing or preparing to implement digital services taxes — fees applied to revenues generated by large tech platforms — and directly follows the ratification of a U.S.-EU trade pact. Trump has previously opposed foreign regulations and taxes targeting American technology companies, and the threat represents one of his most direct economic warnings to trading partners on the issue.

The announcement has significant implications for global trade. A 100 percent tariff could effectively cut off goods from affected countries and reignite the transatlantic trade disputes that have periodically flared during Trump's presidency. European governments have not yet formally responded to the latest threat.

stories.headline: Texas Board Approves Bible Passages as Required Reading in Public Schools, First Such Mandate in Nation
stories.summary:
The Texas State Board of Education on Friday approved a required reading list for more than 5 million public school students that includes passages from the New Testament alongside classic literary works such as Charles Dickens' "Great Expectations." Education observers say the mandate appears to be the first of its kind in the nation, breaking from the tradition of allowing schools or individual teachers to determine reading selections.

The board, which is controlled by Republicans, approved the roughly 200-text list over objections that it lacks diversity and violates the constitutional separation of church and state. Supporters argue that Judeo-Christian traditions were foundational to the nation's founding and should be reflected in public school curricula. The rollout will be staggered, beginning with elementary school students in 2030, and the board was also set to vote Friday on a social studies curriculum linking Bible stories with American history.

Critics, including the progressive Texas Freedom Network, argued that students of all faith backgrounds and none are served by Texas public schools and that elevating a single religious text as required reading sends an exclusionary message. Supporters at the public meeting cited the importance of Christian values in American heritage. Because Texas educates roughly one in ten of the nation's public school students, the decision is expected to draw close national scrutiny and potential legal challenges.

stories.headline: Rep. Massie Warns GOP Faces 'Shellacking' in Midterms, Blasts Party for 'Wasting' Its Majority
stories.summary:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) delivered a sharp rebuke of his own party Thursday, telling reporters outside the Capitol that Republicans are squandering the governing opportunity voters gave them and warning that failure to deliver on their agenda will result in severe midterm losses. "The problem is we're wasting our opportunity that the voters gave us," Massie said. "Republicans are going to pay for that in November. It'll be an absolute shellacking if they don't wake up."

Massie specifically mocked the party's continued focus on election fraud claims despite holding unified control of the House, Senate, Supreme Court, and White House. "I think it's ironic that we control the House, the Senate, the Supreme Court, and the White House, and we're yelling election fraud?" he said. His remarks arrive as President Trump is pressing Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would impose new voter identification requirements. Senate Republicans have acknowledged the bill does not have the 60 votes needed to break a Democratic filibuster, and Trump this week canceled a housing bill-signing ceremony to demand passage of the election legislation first.

The comments carry additional context: Massie lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year following repeated clashes with the White House over spending and foreign policy, yet he has continued to speak publicly and has filed with the FEC, fueling speculation about a 2028 run. The intraparty friction highlighted by Massie's remarks reflects broader GOP tensions over legislative priorities as the midterm election cycle approaches.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Launches One of Its Largest Ever Drone Assaults on Russia, Targeting Crimea and a Dozen Regions
stories.summary:
Ukraine launched a massive overnight drone attack on Russia Friday, with Russian air defenses claiming to have intercepted 660 Ukrainian drones — the largest single Ukrainian drone assault on record, surpassing a previous high of 556 on May 17. Targets spanned a dozen Russian regions, Russian-held Crimea, and surrounding seas, according to Russia's Defense Ministry. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had announced a '40-day influence operation,' believed to refer to a sustained long-range campaign.

Ukraine's Security Service said drones struck Russian naval vessels and air defense radars in the port city of Kerch in Crimea, targeting two reconnaissance and minelaying ships and a cargo-passenger ferry. Russian independent outlet Astra reported fires at a chemical plant and a hydroelectric plant in Novomoskovsk, though the AP could not independently verify the claims. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 47 drones were intercepted approaching the capital, reporting no casualties.

The escalating long-range drone campaign is part of Ukraine's strategy to choke Russian fuel supplies and military logistics, which Western officials and analysts say has stalled Moscow's battlefield efforts and increased pressure on President Vladimir Putin. The strike represents a significant escalation in the scale of Ukrainian offensive operations as the war enters its fifth year.

stories.headline: Mistrial Declared in Arson Case Over 2025 Palisades Fire That Killed 12 and Destroyed Thousands of Homes
stories.summary:
A federal judge declared a mistrial Friday in the arson case against Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, the man accused of sparking the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles after the jury deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal after 13 hours of deliberations. Prosecutors say they intend to retry the case before a new jury, with assistant U.S. attorney Bill Essayli stating the evidence is 'strong' that Rinderknecht ignited the fire on January 1, 2025.

The Palisades Fire ultimately killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes across Pacific Palisades and Malibu, making it one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. Prosecutors argued Rinderknecht, who was driving for Uber that night, started a fire at the Hidden Buddha clearing — a hiking spot near where he dropped off his last passenger — using security camera footage and geolocation data from his phone showing he was at the location around midnight.

Juror No. 4, who voted not guilty, said there was 'just not enough proof,' and questioned whether firefighters bore some responsibility given that witnesses reported seeing smoldering in the area. Defense attorney Steve Haney called the 10-2 split a 'pretty resounding indication' of innocence. Rebuilding in Pacific Palisades has moved slowly, with only 17 homes certified for occupancy since the fire.

stories.headline: Update: Venezuela Earthquake Death Toll Climbs to 589 as Families Search Rubble Without Government Aid
stories.summary:
The death toll from Wednesday's back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela has risen sharply to at least 589, up from earlier reports of 164, with thousands more injured and many still trapped beneath collapsed buildings across northern Venezuela. The 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes struck late Wednesday, causing widespread destruction in the capital Caracas and the coastal state of La Guaira.

Two days after the disaster, desperate families in La Guaira are conducting their own searches through rubble, telling reporters they have not seen state rescue teams despite government claims of a robust response. Residents have been cutting through concrete slabs with power tools in search of trapped relatives, with scenes of grief playing out across flattened neighborhoods.

Acting President Delcy Rodríguez has declared a state of emergency, closed the Caracas airport, and suspended schools and nonessential services. President Trump pledged U.S. support and said he instructed all government agencies to prepare to move quickly; Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the immediate deployment of search and rescue teams, medical resources, and humanitarian assistance.

The earthquakes rank among the strongest to strike Venezuela in more than a century. The gap between official accounts of the government response and what affected residents are reporting on the ground has drawn attention as a major developing dimension of the crisis.

stories.headline: White House Sends Congress $87.6 Billion Supplemental Request to Cover Iran War Costs, Farm Aid, and Ebola Response
stories.summary:
The White House formally submitted an $87.6 billion supplemental spending request to Congress on Wednesday, seeking primarily to replenish the Pentagon following Operation Epic Fury, the U.S.-led military campaign against Iran. The Office of Management and Budget sent the request to House Speaker Mike Johnson, with OMB Director Russ Vought urging Congress to act quickly on what he called urgent priorities.

The bulk of the request is for Defense Department expenses from the Iran war, but it also includes $11.1 billion in economic assistance for American farmers, $1.4 billion for the Ebola outbreak in Central Africa, $1 billion toward construction of a modernized Penn Station in New York City, and $500 million for projects in and around Washington, D.C. The request arrives as the White House is separately pursuing up to $1.5 trillion in overall defense spending — a nearly 50 percent increase over prior levels.

The proposal faces a difficult political path. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of asking taxpayers to "clean up his messes" after what he called a reckless war, while Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, said she would not "rubberstamp tens of billions more for this disastrous war of choice." Many Republican lawmakers have also complained they have yet to receive a formal briefing on the Iran war nearly four months after it began.

The request comes amid ongoing tension between the White House and Congress over Iran war powers. The Senate recently passed a war powers resolution that would halt further hostilities, leading Trump to confront Republican senators directly — including a reported shouting match — over their votes. It remains unclear whether or how quickly Congress will act on the supplemental request.

stories.headline: Small Plane Strikes Beijing's Tallest Skyscraper, Sending Debris Into Streets
stories.summary:
A small aircraft struck the 108-story CITIC Tower — Beijing's tallest building — on Friday night, sending debris raining into the streets of the Chinese capital's central business district. Two witnesses confirmed the crash to Reuters, and videos circulating on social media showed broken windows and falling debris from the skyscraper, which is also known as the China Zun tower.

Crowds in the area fled the falling debris, and a large police presence was deployed around the tower. Chinese authorities had not issued an immediate official statement, and the cause of the incident could not be independently verified as of early reports. The extent of casualties, if any, was not immediately known.

The incident is significant given the tower's location in a dense urban commercial hub and the symbolism of a security breach at one of China's most prominent architectural landmarks. The lack of immediate official comment from Chinese authorities drew notice.

stories.headline: Sierra Leone Holds First-Ever Child Marriage Trial Under 2024 Ban
stories.summary:
Four men appeared in a Freetown High Court on Friday in Sierra Leone's first criminal prosecution under the country's 2024 Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, which banned marriage under age 18. The defendants — including the father of the victim and the man she was married to — face charges of contracting, consenting to, and facilitating child marriage involving a 17-year-old girl.

Three of the four defendants pleaded guilty, but the prosecution reclassified one plea as not guilty after the alleged groom claimed he had obtained the mother's consent under the older Customary Marriage Act, which has since been repealed. If convicted, defendants face a minimum of 15 years in prison, a fine of approximately $4,000, or both. The next hearing is scheduled for July 2.

Sierra Leone's Attorney General Alpha Sesay told the BBC the charges represent "a significant milestone" in enforcing the 2024 law, which struck down customary provisions that had previously allowed parental consent for underage marriages. Gender rights activists celebrated the prosecution as validation of years of legal advocacy. Child marriage has historically been common in Sierra Leone's patriarchal society, and advocates say many cases still go unreported despite the new law.

stories.headline: John Bolton Pleads Guilty to Mishandling Classified Documents, Agrees to $2.25 Million Fine
stories.summary:
Former national security adviser John Bolton entered a guilty plea Friday in federal court in Maryland to one count of illegally retaining sensitive documents, as part of a plea deal reached earlier this month. Bolton agreed to pay a $2.25 million fine. The New York Times reported he could also face prison time.

Bolton's legal jeopardy stemmed from his time as national security adviser under President Trump from 2018 to 2019. Iranian hackers accessed Bolton's personal email account and discovered journal entries containing highly classified information. A grand jury indicted him in October 2025 on 18 counts — eight for transmitting and ten for retaining classified national defense information — after prosecutors found he shared over 1,000 pages of personal records, including classified material at the secret and top-secret levels, with unauthorized individuals believed to be family members.

The investigation spanned two administrations, beginning under Trump's first term and continuing through the Biden years. Bolton is a prominent critic of Trump and authored the 2020 memoir 'The Room Where It Happened,' which Trump previously accused of containing classified disclosures. Trump, asked about Bolton earlier this month, called him "a bad guy" and "a dirty guy."

The case draws inevitable comparisons to the classified documents prosecutions — and subsequent dismissals — pursued against Trump himself, as well as the investigation into President Biden's handling of classified materials. Legal observers note that Bolton's plea underscores that classified document cases can result in criminal accountability regardless of the defendant's political affiliation.

stories.headline: Christmas Market Attacker Sentenced to Life in Prison for Killing Six in Magdeburg, Germany
stories.summary:
A German court sentenced Taleb Al-Abdulmohsen, 51, to life in prison Friday for the December 2024 vehicle-ramming attack on a Christmas market in Magdeburg that killed six people — including a nine-year-old boy — and injured approximately 300 others. The court imposed the maximum available sentence after finding him guilty of murder.

Prosecutors said Al-Abdulmohsen drove a rented BMW at speeds up to 48 km/h through the crowded market on December 20, 2024, in an attack lasting just over a minute. Prosecutors said he planned the attack well in advance and acted alone. A psychiatric expert testified that Al-Abdulmohsen suffers from narcissistic personality disorder and an overwhelming need for attention.

Al-Abdulmohsen, a Saudi national who was granted asylum in Germany in 2016, told the court he was motivated by grievances against German authorities and anger over the treatment of Saudi women. Prosecutors said he was not driven by serious ideological goals but primarily by personal motives. He had previously worked as a psychiatrist at a secure facility in Bernburg and had expressed support on social media for the far-right Alternative for Germany party.

The verdict closes the criminal proceedings on one of the deadliest attacks on German soil in recent years, though Al-Abdulmohsen retains the right to appeal. The case prompted extensive debate in Germany about asylum policy and the monitoring of individuals with documented grievances against the state.

stories.headline: Update: Trump's Voter-Fraud Legislative Push Stalls as Courts Block Executive Orders and Senate Defies SAVE Act
stories.summary:
President Trump's campaign to tighten voting laws ahead of the November 2026 midterms is encountering significant legal and legislative resistance. Federal courts have blocked multiple election-related executive orders, and Senate Republicans have refused to advance the SAVE Act, which would require proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote.

Trump has retaliated against Senate Republicans who blocked the measure, threatening to withhold his signature from legislation they support. The standoff comes as Trump separately canceled a planned housing bill signing earlier this week, demanding voter ID legislation be passed first — an indication of how central election integrity measures have become to his second-term agenda.

Supporters of the SAVE Act argue that verifying citizenship at registration is a common-sense safeguard against noncitizen voting, which they contend is an underreported problem. Opponents, including most Democrats and some federal judges, argue that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare, that existing safeguards are sufficient, and that such requirements would disenfranchise eligible voters who lack the required documents.

With midterm elections roughly five months away, the political stakes are high. Trump commented Thursday on the results of New York Democratic primaries, in which progressive candidates backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani won several races, warning that "the Communists are finally making their move" — framing the 2026 cycle as a defining ideological contest.

stories.headline: New York City Rent Guidelines Board Votes to Freeze Rents on One Million Stabilized Apartments
stories.summary:
New York City's Rent Guidelines Board voted 7-1 Thursday to freeze rents on approximately one million rent-stabilized apartments across all five boroughs, a central campaign pledge of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist who took office earlier this year. The freeze will apply to both one- and two-year leases in rent-stabilized buildings from October 2026 through September 2027.

The vote was preceded by the resignation of board member Christina Smyth, one of three appointees of former Mayor Eric Adams, who accused the panel of bias and said the outcome had been "predetermined" by the mayor. Smyth said the board had "knowingly disregarded its own evidence" showing landlords face rising operating costs. Mamdani had appointed six of the board's seven remaining members after taking office.

Tenant advocates cheered the decision, arguing that incomes have not kept pace with inflation and that prior rent increases had not translated into building improvements. The board's chair said the decision reflected data showing that most tenants in rent-stabilized housing "struggle to meet basic affordability thresholds."

Landlord groups warned of serious consequences. James Whelan, president of the Real Estate Board of New York, said the freeze would reduce investment in maintenance and accelerate the deterioration of the city's housing stock. The decision marks a significant early policy victory for Mamdani, whose election signaled a leftward shift in New York City politics and drew national attention as a test of democratic socialist governance in the country's largest city.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Confronts GOP Sen. Cassidy Over Iran War Powers Vote, Then Grants Briefing
stories.summary:
President Trump clashed openly with Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) during a closed-door Republican Senate lunch Wednesday, calling the senator a "lunatic" after Cassidy stood to challenge Trump on the lack of congressional briefings about the ongoing Iran military operation. Cassidy, one of four Republicans who backed a war powers resolution the previous day seeking to limit further U.S. action against Iran, told Trump the operation had lasted four months rather than the promised four weeks and that original objectives had not been achieved. Trump repeatedly told Cassidy to sit down; Cassidy acknowledged losing his temper but said he matched Trump's tone.

Within hours of the confrontation, Cassidy received an invitation to the White House for a classified briefing with Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff. After the briefing, Cassidy reversed course, casting a late-night vote against a similar war powers resolution — this time helping Republicans successfully block the measure.

The episode is a notable departure from the pattern of most congressional Republicans, who have largely avoided public confrontations with Trump during his second term. Cassidy's initial stand reflected growing unease among some GOP members about the scope and duration of military action against Iran without formal congressional authorization or robust public disclosure.

The exchange is a new development on previously covered tensions between Trump and Senate Republicans over Iran, with the Cassidy confrontation, subsequent White House briefing, and reversed vote all occurring Wednesday — materially changing the situation from prior coverage.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strikes Russian Natural Gas Plant and Satellite Centers in Escalating Long-Range Campaign
stories.summary:
Ukrainian forces struck a major natural gas processing plant and two satellite communications centers inside Russia overnight, Ukraine's General Staff announced Wednesday. The strikes are part of an intensifying aerial campaign targeting Russian energy infrastructure and military industries as Kyiv deploys longer-range weapons of its own manufacture. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia has responded by redeploying some air defense systems from Russian regions to Moscow and to the Kerch Bridge in Crimea, a critical supply link for Russian forces.

Zelenskyy also warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin has been stepping up efforts to draw Belarus more deeply into the war, with Ukrainian officials ordering a mandatory evacuation of communities in the Chernihiv region bordering Belarus starting July 1. Zelenskyy has accepted an unconditional ceasefire proposed by President Trump; Putin has refused.

The strikes represent a continued escalation in Ukraine's strategy of hitting Russian territory to pressure Moscow's war economy, even as diplomatic efforts remain stalled. The redeployment of Russian air defenses to protect the Kerch Bridge suggests Kyiv's long-range strikes are achieving strategic effects on Russian logistics.

stories.headline: Judge Orders DOJ to Release Unredacted Epstein Files or Explain Why It Cannot by July 2
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., ordered the Justice Department on Thursday to release additional unredacted Jeffrey Epstein records or provide a legal explanation by July 2 for why they must remain sealed. U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan issued the preliminary injunction in a lawsuit filed by attorney and independent journalist Katie Phang, who alleges the DOJ failed to comply with records release obligations. The order targets specific high-interest documents, including at least eight email exchanges referenced in the Epstein files.

The ruling could force the public disclosure of previously withheld details from the Epstein investigation, or compel the government to publicly justify continued secrecy over specific materials. The Epstein files have been a subject of intense public interest, with Congress and various advocacy groups pressing for full transparency about the late financier's network and any potential co-conspirators.

The DOJ now faces a one-week deadline to act. If it cannot comply, it must present the court with a legally sufficient explanation — a process that would itself put the government's justifications for secrecy on the public record.

stories.headline: Update: Reflecting Pool Liner Was Cut With Sharp Knife, National Park Service Court Filing Says
stories.summary:
A National Park Service official stated in a court filing Thursday that the liner of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was damaged by a cut from a sharp knife or razor, providing the first official public account of how the pool was damaged. Deputy Director of Operations Frank Lands said a U.S. Park Police report documented the cut through caulk over foam sealant, as well as approximately 70 fence post tops thrown into the pool. Five people have been arrested and five others cited for vandalism in connection with the incident.

President Trump had earlier this week claimed vandals caused "a 300-foot-long gash" and alleged fertilizer was put in the water, vowing to provide evidence in court. A previous AP review found that evidence contradicted elements of Trump's account. The NPS filing confirms physical damage occurred but does not specify when it happened or identify suspects.

The pool was drained and refitted with a tinted polyurea liner as part of a multi-million dollar renovation Trump ordered ahead of the nation's 250th anniversary. After being refilled, the pool experienced an algae bloom and discoloration issues. The NPS plans to drain it again after July 4th celebrations to conduct repairs and assess the full extent of damage to the liner.
